meta.topic: Designing discovery for a new product

problem:
Meridian Bank wants to launch an instant payment product for small business customers, and the product sponsor has asked the team to make payments faster. The request has no named user group, no baseline, no target speed and no statement of the problem customers actually face today. Small businesses currently pay suppliers through standard credit transfers that arrive later in the day, and some use card payments that carry higher fees, but nobody has measured how often a slow payment causes a real business cost such as a missed supplier discount or a delayed shipment. The bank already offers instant euro payments under the SCT Inst scheme, which has no scheme-level maximum amount since the 2025 rulebook change and must complete within 10 seconds, with Verification of Payee mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025. Those scheme facts shape what is technically possible, but they do not tell the team which customers need the product or what success looks like.

The discovery team has six weeks before the funding decision and must produce a recommendation the investment committee can trust. The team includes a business analyst, a product manager, a payments architect and an operations lead, and each of them holds a different view of what faster means. The architect wants to expose the existing instant rail through an API, the operations lead worries about fraud screening inside a 10-second window, and the sponsor wants a launch date. Without a disciplined discovery phase the bank risks building a technically correct product that solves nobody's urgent problem, or promising a speed the fraud and screening controls cannot support. The case asks the learner to run discovery properly: define target users, state the problem, form testable hypotheses, record constraints, define a minimum viable product and agree success metrics before any build commitment is made.
solution:
Start by naming the target users precisely, for example small businesses that pay domestic suppliers on fixed weekly cycles, and exclude segments the product will not serve in the first release. Write a problem statement in the form of who suffers, what it costs them, and how often, then gather evidence: payment volumes, current settlement times, supplier discount losses, and support contacts about late payments. Form hypotheses that can be tested, such as that suppliers offer early payment discounts that customers miss because standard transfers arrive too late, and test each one with data or customer interviews rather than opinion.

Map the current journey from payment initiation to supplier receipt, mark every wait, manual step and failure point, and record the baseline: median and worst-case times, failure rates and costs. Then define the target state in measurable terms, for example 95 percent of eligible instant payments completed within 10 seconds with a defined fraud-screening pass rate, and state which rails, currencies, channels, amounts and customer segments are in scope. Record constraints explicitly: the 10-second SCT Inst execution limit, mandatory Verification of Payee, fraud and sanctions screening, cut-offs, and the fact that PSD2 remains the law in force while PSD3 is not law. Finally define the MVP as the smallest release that proves the value hypothesis, list what is deliberately excluded, and agree success metrics, owners and the evidence the investment committee will see at the funding gate.

decision.question: Meridian Bank has six weeks of discovery time for a new instant payment product for small businesses. The sponsor wants faster payments but has not defined the user, the problem or the success measure. You are the business analyst and must recommend what discovery should deliver before the funding decision.

options.label: A
options.detail: Interview only the sponsor and the architect, then write requirements from their combined view of what faster means.

options.label: B
options.detail: Skip discovery and start building an instant payment API, since the SCT Inst rail already exists and speed is the obvious requirement.

options.label: C
options.detail: Promise a 10-second end-to-end payment for every customer and every amount, then design fraud controls afterwards.

options.label: D
options.detail: Run structured discovery: define target users, state the problem, test hypotheses with evidence, record constraints, define the MVP and agree measurable success metrics.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because discovery exists to turn a vague goal into a testable, measurable product decision. Option B builds before knowing who benefits or what success means. Option A relies on two internal opinions and ignores customers, operations and risk. Option C commits to a speed target before checking whether screening, Verification of Payee and fraud controls can fit inside the 10-second execution window.

steps.title: Sponsor discovery kick-off and agree decision date and funding gate
Define target user segments and draft problem statement with evidence sources
Interview small business customers and map current payment journey
Document rail capabilities, SCT Inst 10-second limit and Verification of Payee requirement
Quantify current failure rates, manual work and support contacts
Draft testable hypotheses and agree success metrics with sponsor and risk
Define MVP scope and exclusions and present recommendation to investment committee

happy: Discovery ends with a signed-off problem statement, an evidence-backed hypothesis set, a measured baseline, a measurable target, an agreed MVP scope with exclusions, and success metrics with owners. The investment committee funds the MVP knowing which customers it serves, what it must achieve, and which constraints bound the design.

negative.title: Stakeholders disagree on what faster means
negative.detail: The sponsor, architect and operations lead each define speed differently. Facilitate a workshop that anchors faster to a measured customer outcome and a numeric target, and record dissent and the decision.

negative.title: Speed conflicts with fraud controls
negative.detail: Screening and Verification of Payee cannot fit inside the 10-second window for some payments. Define which payments are eligible for instant execution, which route to a slower rail, and how the customer is told before submission.

negative.title: No customer evidence supports the hypothesis
negative.detail: Interviews and data show late payments rarely cost customers money. Report the finding honestly, recommend stopping or pivoting the product, and do not manufacture a business case.

negative.title: Scheme rule changes mid-discovery
negative.detail: A rulebook update changes a limit, deadline or mandatory field. Run rule impact analysis across channels, validation and operations, and re-baseline the target before the funding decision.

technical: Keep a single discovery record with traceability from problem statement to hypothesis to evidence to requirement. Store baseline measurements with their source, date and query so they can be re-run. Version the scope and exclusions, and record every assumption with an owner and a validation date. Do not store customer interview notes with personal data beyond what is needed, and keep the decision log as the audit trail for the funding gate.

accounting: Discovery itself has no customer debit or credit, but the business case must quantify the financial effect of the target state: earlier supplier receipt, discount capture, reduced late-payment fees and lower manual handling. Operations must be staffed for the new failure modes, including payments rejected by Verification of Payee and payments that exceed the instant window and fall back to another rail. Define the worklists, service levels and reconciliation points for those exceptions before the build starts, so the MVP launch does not create an unstaffed queue.

scenarios.given: a vague objective to make payments faster,
scenarios.then: an agreed measurable target and the in-scope payment journeys are documented.

scenarios.given: a hypothesis about missed supplier discounts,
scenarios.then: the hypothesis is confirmed, refuted or revised with named evidence.
fraud screening and Verification of Payee steps are shown to fit inside the limit or the payment is routed elsewhere.

questions.question: What is the first thing discovery must produce for a vague product request?
options: A measurable problem statement with named target users
questions.explanation: Discovery must first establish who suffers, what it costs and how often, otherwise every later decision rests on an untested assumption.

questions.question: Under the current SCT Inst rules, which statement about the scheme maximum is correct?
options: There is no scheme-level maximum since the 2025 rulebook change
The maximum depends on the customer segment
questions.explanation: The EUR 100,000 scheme maximum was removed by the EPC SCT Inst Rulebook 2025, effective 5 October 2025, so no scheme-level maximum now applies.

questions.question: Why must Verification of Payee be part of the discovery constraints?
options: It only applies to direct debits
It is optional for instant payments
It is mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025 and affects the 10-second journey
questions.explanation: Verification of Payee is mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025, so the journey, timing and failure handling must include it.

questions.question: What should the team do if customer evidence refutes the core hypothesis?
options: Hide the evidence from the investment committee
Report the finding honestly and recommend stopping or pivoting
questions.explanation: Discovery exists to test hypotheses with evidence, and a refuted hypothesis is a valid outcome that prevents wasted build spend.
